meta.name: Reverse Engineer Lab
meta.description: An independent catalog of reverse engineering research.

data.title: Digits: source transactions and the ledger are different layers
data.target_version: Connect API v1; public documentation reviewed 2026-10-30
data.question: How does raw transaction ingestion relate to the accounting ledger?
data.summary: Digits exposes a source layer for incoming financial records and a ledger layer for processed accounting results. That separation is the useful contract: ingestion is not a promise that a matching ledger entry is immediately available.
data.observed: The public documentation distinguishes Sources from the Ledger. Source records retain external identifiers; matching groups records that represent the same economic event. The Connect API exposes separate source-transaction and ledger read operations.
data.inferred: This boundary suggests that a consumer should distinguish receipt of source data from completion of bookkeeping processing. That is an interpretation of the documented model, not a measurement of processing latency.
data.unknown: Public documentation analysis only. No customer ledger, authenticated account, processing-latency test, or internal implementation is published here.
data.author: Reverse Engineer Lab
data.models: Source, external identifier, transaction and ledger are distinct concepts. A source record is evidence of an upstream event; a ledger view represents its accounting treatment.

data.title: Campfire: journal entries and bank-feed ingestion have separate roles
data.question: Which accounting objects anchor Campfire’s integration surface?
data.summary: Campfire exposes journal-entry workflows alongside bank-feed ingestion, bills and invoices. The public contract also documents a bank-sync mode that records transactions without immediately creating journals.
data.observed: The API documentation includes journal-entry creation, accounts-payable and accounts-receivable workflows. Its bank-feed endpoint documents an optional skip-journal behavior. OAuth apps and webhooks are separate integration features.
data.inferred: The separation makes a bank transaction and its eventual accounting journal different lifecycle objects. A successful feed import alone should not be read as proof of a posted journal.
data.unknown: This entry describes public contracts, not the vendor’s database schema or customer configuration. It does not establish reconciliation accuracy, authorization behavior, or transaction atomicity through runtime testing.
data.author: Reverse Engineer Lab

data.title: DOSS: workflows connect records, events and operational decisions
data.question: What is the public boundary between DOSS data and workflow automation?
data.summary: DOSS presents operational workflows as event- or schedule-triggered processes over shared data. Public examples connect purchase-order approval, order routing and document matching rather than treating each module as a separate automation product.
data.observed: The public workflow page describes branching, iteration, formulas, document parsing, AI steps and execution logs. The platform separately presents inventory, order management and shared master-data modules.
data.inferred: The published interface suggests a configurable process layer over operational records. It does not, by itself, prove a particular database engine, graph representation, execution guarantee or transaction model.
data.unknown: Coverage is the publicly described product contract. The detailed customer documentation requires authentication; no private customer data, captured session, or unsupported internal schema is included.
data.author: Reverse Engineer Lab
data.workflows: The documented examples use events or schedules to trigger steps, with conditional branches and a visible execution history. The exact retry and concurrency guarantees remain unverified.

data.title: Katana: stock on hand, committed and expected are separate quantities
data.question: Why can a single inventory number fail to explain product availability?
data.summary: Katana’s inventory model distinguishes on-hand, committed and expected stock per variant and location. This exposes future obligations and incoming supply separately from what is physically held.
data.observed: The inventory object documents quantity_in_stock, quantity_committed and quantity_expected. Sales and manufacturing orders create commitments; purchasing and manufacturing contribute expected supply. A sales-order row can link to a make-to-order manufacturing order.
data.inferred: Availability is a relationship among stock, demand and future supply rather than one universal count. The API model alone does not prove reservation ordering or race-free allocation.
data.unknown: Public schema and workflow analysis. No live warehouse or order was changed. Costing behavior, concurrent reservations and exception handling were not reproduced.
data.author: Reverse Engineer Lab
data.models: Inventory is identified by product/material variant and location. Quantities track physical stock, commitments and expected replenishment separately.

data.title: Shiptheory: shipment booking sits behind service selection and shipping rules
data.question: How does Shiptheory separate shipment data from carrier-service decisions?
data.summary: Shiptheory provides one API surface for shipment booking, labels, available services and shipping rules. The useful distinction is between describing a shipment and choosing how a carrier should handle it.
data.observed: The public API documentation covers creating and searching shipments, delivery-service lists, package sizes, labels and return labels. The product API page describes rules based on destination, order value, product, weight and SKU.
data.inferred: A shipment record, service-selection decision and returned label are distinct outputs of the workflow. Receiving an API response should not be treated as evidence that a parcel has physically moved.
data.unknown: Documentation-level coverage; no paid label, carrier booking, shipment cancellation or physical-delivery test was performed for this public entry. Carrier-specific behavior and account configuration may differ.
data.author: Reverse Engineer Lab

data.title: Shopify: GraphQL query cost and cursor pagination define the read contract
data.target_version: Admin GraphQL API 2026-10; public documentation reviewed 2026-10-30
data.question: How do Shopify’s API limits differ from a flat requests-per-minute model?
data.summary: Shopify’s Admin GraphQL API budgets query cost rather than treating every request as equal. Cursor pagination is a separate boundary: advancing a list requires its page information, not an invented numeric offset.
data.observed: The public limits documentation distinguishes calculated GraphQL query cost from REST request buckets and Storefront protections. GraphQL responses expose cost and throttle information; the pagination guide documents cursors and pageInfo.
data.inferred: Two requests can consume different capacity even when their HTTP shapes look similar. Pagination and throttling therefore need separate interpretation. This entry does not benchmark a store or plan.
data.unknown: Public API contract analysis. No merchant identifiers, private store state, authenticated traces or pending research additions are included. Live capacity can vary by API, plan and platform conditions.
data.author: Reverse Engineer Lab
data.apis: The documented GraphQL read surface uses query selections and connections. Throttle metadata describes available query capacity; pageInfo describes position within a connection.

data.title: Klaviyo: API revision and rate-limit tier are explicit contract inputs
data.question: What determines the behavior and throughput of a Klaviyo API call?
data.summary: Klaviyo versions its API with dated revision headers and publishes endpoint-specific rate limits. Treating every endpoint as one timeless contract or one shared throughput limit loses information present in the interface.
data.observed: The changelog identifies revision 2026-10-15 and documents endpoint changes. The developer documentation separates burst and steady rate limits and describes responses for rate-limit errors.
data.inferred: A stored request description needs its revision as well as its endpoint to be reproducible. A caller’s queueing behavior must account for the endpoint’s documented limit tier rather than just counting all calls together.
data.unknown: Public documentation and schema-level analysis. No profile, consent record, message, campaign or customer account was accessed or changed. This does not verify delivery, attribution or identity-merging behavior.
data.author: Reverse Engineer Lab

data.title: WooCommerce: storefront API and order storage are independent boundaries
data.target_version: WooCommerce 11.2.1 research baseline; Store API v1 documentation
data.question: Does the presence of the Store API determine how orders are stored?
data.summary: WooCommerce separates its customer-facing Store API from its order-storage implementation. A storefront API route and the choice between legacy posts and High-Performance Order Storage answer different questions.
data.observed: The Store API documents product, cart and checkout operations scoped to a customer session. HPOS documents dedicated order tables and a compatibility/synchronization path from posts-based storage. The public guidance distinguishes the Store API from the authenticated management REST API.
data.inferred: A route inventory alone cannot establish which storage engine is authoritative, and storage selection alone does not establish which checkout interface a storefront uses.
data.unknown: Only public platform contracts are described. No merchant domain, extension inventory, customer data or production configuration is included. Compatibility and live checkout behavior must be established per installation.
data.author: Reverse Engineer Lab
data.models: The cart and checkout are session-facing resources. HPOS stores orders in purpose-built tables while compatibility mode can synchronize legacy representations.

data.title: Notion: a database container is not the same as a data source
data.question: What changed when Notion introduced multi-source databases?
data.summary: Notion split the database container from the data sources it contains. The practical consequence is that database identity alone no longer identifies a single queryable schema in every case.
data.observed: The upgrade guide introduces first-class multi-source databases. It directs clients to discover data_source_id values and use them for operations that previously relied on database_id, including page parents, queries and relations.
data.inferred: A container-level identifier and a schema-bearing data-source identifier have different jobs. Assuming one source per database is a compatibility assumption, not a timeless platform invariant.
data.unknown: Public API migration analysis, not a claim about the internal storage engine. No private workspace, record map, billing data, agent vault or authenticated capture is published. Later API versions may add further changes.
data.author: Reverse Engineer Lab
